list.listitem: The diagnosis of attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is made on the basis of reports of behavior and symptoms and not by specific testing. Use the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders 5th Edition criteria for diagnosis.C
Diagnostic tests are not routinely indicated in the diagnosis of ADHD.B
Treat ADHD as a chronic condition requiring continuous treatment.C
A stimulant should be the initial choice of medication.A
Focused counseling—whether educational, vocational, problem-solving, or anger management—is recommended.B
If improvement in ADHD symptoms is not seen with appropriate management and adherence to treatment plan, evaluate the patient for the presence of coexisting conditions.A

background.definition: Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is a developmentally inappropriate lack of attention and/or hyperactivity and impulsivity that interferes with an individual's daily life.

list.listitem: The worldwide prevalence noted in 2007 was 5.3%.
A more recent meta-analysis in 2015 notes the prevalence to be 7.2%.
The distribution appears to be equal between male and female patients even though more males are diagnosed in early childhood.
The annual societal cost of ADHD in childhood and adolescence is an estimated 42.5 billion dollars with a range of 36 billion dollars to 52.4 billion dollars.
ADHD is the most common neurobehavioral condition in children. It is also among the most prevalent chronic health conditions that affect school-aged children.
The etiology of ADHD is complex and multifactorial. No single risk factor is sufficient.
Molecular genetic studies suggest that the genetic architecture of ADHD is complex even though twin studies estimate the heritability to be 76%.
ADHD may be an additional deleterious outcome of prenatal exposure to alcohol and/or nicotine products..
Symptoms consistent with ADHD can result from traumatic brain injury.
Low birth weight is a significant risk factor for ADHD.
Population-based birth cohort data indicate that former late preterm infants have similar rates of Learning Disabilities and ADHD as term infants.
Digital media use is associated with ADHD symptoms in adolescents. It is not known if limiting use decreases symptoms.
Lead exposure may be associated with inattention.
Adverse childhood experiences may increase odds of developing ADHD.
Prenatal acetaminophen exposure is not associated with a risk of ADHD.

Recent magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) studies show different morphology in prefrontal lobes, smaller volume of the white matter of the right frontal lobe, and smaller volume of the left caudate head.
N-acetylaspartate depletion in the prefrontal cortex has been proposed as a cause.
Metabolic activity is decreased in the frontal lobe as shown by functional MRI.
Population screening in otherwise healthy children is not recommended by any professional organization.C

When doing any mental health assessment, the clinician should screen for ADHD by specifically asking about inattention, impulsivity, and hyperactivity, and asking whether such symptoms cause impairment.B
The diagnosis is made using the explicit criteria from DSM-V.C
It is important to obtain information on the individual in more than one setting, especially at school for children.B
Be aware of coexisting conditions, which can make the diagnosis more difficult and complicate treatment.C
Diagnostic tests are not routinely indicated in the diagnosis of ADHD.B

Differential.Differential_Features: Generally has a recent history or a clear start of the symptoms
A clear start of the symptoms with a history of head trauma
Anhedonia, persistent dysphoria, and sleep disturbance
Delusions, prolonged sleep or awake periods, and persistent euphoric or dysphoric mood
Somatic disorders of anxiety, constant apprehension and/or worry
Antisocial behavior, self-injurious—borderline behavior, hard to distinguish at times, and poor insight that behavior is self-defeating
Hyperdynamic physical findings (ie, hyperreflexic, goiter, tachycardia, etc) and positive laboratory findings
A progressive increase in symptoms after an emotionally traumatic event or chronic toxic stress

list.listitem: See for the DSM-V diagnostic criteria for ADHD.

Children: Suspect ADHD if parents are concerned about inattention, impulsivity, overactivity, or ADHD by name. A systematic review of 8 studies concluded that both teachers and parents have moderately good diagnostic accuracy.
Adults: Suspect ADHD if the patient is concerned about inattention, impulsivity, and hyperactivity with history dating back before the age of 12 years. May present with anxiety/depression.
Evaluate overall physical appearance for any different genetic expression (eg, low-set ears), as well as signs and symptoms of abuse.

Measure height and weight, blood pressure, and pulse. Perform a neurologic examination (asymmetry of reflexes, soft signs such as fine/gross motor function and clumsy, expressive language). Evaluate developmental status, screen hearing and vision, and examine thyroid.
Evaluate for comorbid behavioral conditions such as depression, anxiety, conduct disorder, and oppositional defiant disorder. Apply DSM-V criteria to confirm the diagnosis ().
Evaluate for comorbid physical conditions such as tics and sleep apnea.
Evaluate for comorbid development conditions such as learning and language disorders and autism spectrum disorders.
Screening tools are of uncertain effectiveness in ADHD.
The Connors Abbreviated Symptom Questionaire is 83% sensitive and 84% specific and may be the most effective tool in diagnosing ADHD.
Consider screening for substance use in adolenscents as certain substances can mimic ADHD symptoms.
Lead or thyroid studies, imaging studies or electroencephalography, and computerized performance tests are not recommended for the routine evaluation of ADHD.
Complete neuropsychology testing is not recommended unless there is a positive screening result for learning disability, borderline low IQ, or central nervous system disease or injury.
EEGs are innacurate in diagnosing ADHD.
A screening instrument has been developed and validated in adults.
The new World Health Organization Adult Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder self-report screening scale for DSM-5 is short, easily scored, detects the vast majority of general population cases.
The general approach in children and early adolescents is shown in .

Assessment of ADHD in children requires evidence directly obtained from parents or caregivers and teachers or school-based professionals regarding core symptoms of ADHD in various settings, the age of onset, duration of symptoms, and degree of impairment. Parent-based diagnosis of ADHD is as accurate as a teacher-base diagnosis.
Diagnostic testing is not routinely recommended.
The general approach in adults and late adolescents is shown in .
Symptoms in adults should be present in more than one setting and assessment requires evidence from multiple informants. Current neuropsychological tests have limited diagnostic value.
Establish a treatment program that recognizes ADHD as a chronic condition.C
Educate the individuals and their families about the disorder. Involve children, teachers, and other significant individuals in this education, that is, use a team approach.C
Encourage regular physical activity.C
A psychostimulant is the cornerstone of initial pharmacotherapy.A
For children ages 4-6 years old with ADHD, parent-training in behavioral management (PTBM) is first-line therapy.A
Focused counseling—whether educational, vocational, problem solving, or anger management—is recommended.B
If improvement in ADHD symptoms is not seen with appropriate management and adherence to treatment plan, evaluate for the presence of coexisting conditions.A
Treat ADHD as a chronic condition with a strategy of long-term management. Treatment should be consistent from day-to-day to address behavior in all settings and not just for school performance only.

Drug treatment of ADHD is associated with a small decrease in important clinical outcomes including suicidal behavior and substance misuse in children and adults, and transport-associated accidents and criminality in those older than 15 years.

An umbrella systematic review concluded based on moderate to high certainty evidence that alpha-2 agonists, amphetamines, atomoxetine, methylphenidate, and viloxazine show medium to large effect sizes in reducing the severity of ADHD symptoms in children and adolescents.
In adults, atomoxetine, methylphenidate, and amphetamines are effective to improve ADHD symptoms.
Medications and behavioral interventions can improve symptoms but may not have an effect on function or school performance. There are not many trials that compare medications head to head.

In children and adolescents, the initial medication of choice is a psychostimulant (). Start at a low dosage (doses are not usually weight dependent) and titrate as needed in 2-week to 4-week intervals. Systematic follow-up to monitor target outcomes should be established along with monitoring for side effects such as weight loss, anorexia, and insomnia. If an individual fails to respond to one stimulant, then there is a good chance that he/she will respond to an alternate stimulant.

Carefully monitored medical treatment is likely to be more cost-effective in the routine treatment of children with ADHD, particularly those without comorbid disorders, than no treatment with medication.
Medications for ADHD do not increase cardiovascular risks.
There is no association between stimulant treatment for ADHD and subsequent substance use.
Adolescents and young adults treated with amphetamine have a slightly higher risk of psychosis than those treated with methylphenidate. The absolute risk is 0.21% vs. 0.1% (NNH=909).

Atomoxetine (Strattera) is superior to placebo for the treatment of ADHD but has not been directly compared with stimulants. The major side effects are nausea, anorexia, sedation, and/or sleep disturbance. In patients with an active substance abuse problem, comorbid anxiety or tics, consider atomoxetine as the first-line medication. In children who respond to the typical dosage of atomoxetine (1.2 mg/kg/d), a lowered dosage of 0.5 mg/kg/d is similarly effective in maintaining scores on a validated measurement scale.
There appears to be no clinically relevant difference between fast and slow switching from stimulants to atomoxetine.
Atomoxetine may provide slight benefit in children 5 to 6 years of age with at least moderately severe disease.
A pilot study suggests that a stimulant and atomoxetine may be used together with caution and close monitoring, but only when there is inadequate response to stimulant medication alone.

Clonidine or guanfacine (Tenex) is useful in children who exhibit disruptive or explosive behavior. Side effects include sedation, low blood pressure, and/or rebound hypertension (when discontinued). In a recent study involving patients between the ages of 6 years and 17 years, extended-release guanfacine showed significant improvement in hyperactivity/impulsivity and inattention in all dosage groups (2, 3, or 4 mg/d) compared with placebo.

Desipramine appears to be both safe and effective in the treatment of children with ADHD complicated by chronic tic disorders. The use of methylphenidate and clonidine together is effective in children who have the combination of ADHD and Tourette's syndrome.
Treatment of ADHD with stimulant medication neither protects nor increases the risk of later substance use disorders.
Metadoxine (extended release) may be effective in treating inattentive symptoms in selected adults with ADHD (predominantly inattentive type).
In adults with ADHD, methylphenidate, atomoxetine, or desipramine (Norpramin) are similarly effective. In addition, sustained-release bupropion is effective in the treatment of adult ADHD.
Among adults with ADHD and clinically significant executive function deficits, lisdexamfetamine was associates with significant improvements in self-reported executive function ratings.
Adults on stimulant therapy for ADHD may be at risk for a resting heart rate >90 beats per minute.
Consistent stimulant therapy for ADHD may decrease smoking risk.

Polyunsaturated fatty acids do not improve parent rated ADHD symptoms according to high certainty evidence.There is limited data that combined omega-3 and omega-6 fatty acid supplementation improved school behavior and performance in short-term studies.
Diet modification is not recommended in ADHD.
Yoga may have added benefit in boys with ADHD stabilized on medication.
Melatonin (3-6 mg at bedtime) may be helpful for children and adolescents with ADHD who have sleeping problems.
Megavitamins should not given to children with ADHD because of their ineffectiveness and potentially serious side effects.
There are no high-quality randomized controlled trials assessing the benefit of acupuncture in ADHD.
Magnesium is currently not recommended for treating ADHD.
Cannabidiol oil is not recommended.

Clinical experience suggests that daily physical activity is beneficial for patients with ADHD at all ages, despite sparse scientific data. A preliminary study shows that exercise may effect dopaminergic-like responses in children with ADHD by reducing motor impersistence. Motor impersistence is related to behavioral disinhibition, which is a hallmark feature of ADHD.
A meta-analysis showed anxiety and depressive symptoms improved in children with ADHD, but improvement in hyperactive/impulsive and inattention symptoms were not statistically significant.
The effectiveness of family therapy intervention is inconclusive.
Parent training in behavioral management (PTBM) interventions are recommended for children ages 4 years to 12 years.

In the adult with ADHD, the evidence of the effects of psychotherapy is sparse. Clinical experience suggests that cognitive behavioral therapy may be helpful along with special coaching related to time management, organizational skills, financial management, and so forth. Cognitive training is not recommended by the American Academy of Pediatrics.
Cognitive behavioral therapy is effective in adults to improve symptoms of ADHD.
CHADD (Children and Adults with ADHD) is an excellent resource for information on the disorder and local group support.
Neurofeedback appears to show significant academic performance improvements in children 7 to 14 years of age.
Neurofeedback is a promising attention training modality for children ages 7 to 11 with ADHD.
In contrast, a systematic review found minimal benefit of neurofeedback for individuals of any age with ADHD.
Sleep counseling may improve sleep and symptoms in children with ADHD.
Mindfulness-based interventions may improve inattention and hyperactivity.
There is little evidence to support the routine recommendation of the highly restrictive Feingold diet.
Food colorings and additives increase global hyperactivity in some 3- to 4-year-olds and some 8- to 9-year-olds.

Educate individuals and their family about the disorder. Involve children, teachers, and other significant individuals in this education. Be aware of the impact of the diagnosis of ADHD on the adult patient's self-esteem.
Educational interventions are recommended and may include Individualized Education Plan (IEP) or a rehabilitation plan (504 plan).
Technology-assisted quality improvement (QI) intervention improved some ADHD care quality and resulted in additional reductions in parent-related ADHD symptoms among patients with ADHD.

Treatment will most likely be continuous, with possible fluctuations in dosage, change in medications, or occasional drug holidays (weekends, vacations, etc) in children. Because the behavioral impact of the disease is present in multiple situations, continuous treatment (especially in adults) is preferred.
As a child advances through adolescence into adulthood, you may consider weaning the patient off medication and evaluating symptomatology.
The following may warrant consultation: oppositional defiant disorder (35%), conduct disorder (26%), anxiety disorders (26%), mood disorders/depression (18%), and/or learning disabilities (12%-25%).
Minimize insomnia by avoiding late afternoon/evening dosing or by changing formulation (see ).
If mood lability or tics are a problem with stimulants, atomoxetine is a better option.
At least two-thirds of children with ADHD will still have the disorder as an adult.A
ADHD is a lifelong disorder, which will require varying degrees of intervention. Systematic follow-up should be provided to assess the results of those interventions.C
In children with ADHD, at least two-thirds will still experience symptoms into adulthood.
Low self-esteem and difficulty with social/interpersonal skills are likely to occur in patients with ADHD.
Frequent job changes and difficulty maintaining relationships are typical.

Individuals with ADHD have an elevated risk for antisocial, mood, and anxiety disorders. Longitudinal results show more impaired intellectual and achievement scores; in addition, these individual have more impaired school, interpersonal, and family functioning at follow-up.
Drug use in adulthood is mainly related to a lifetime coexistence of conduct disorder with ADHD and is associated with the severity of drug use in adolescence.
The obvious physical hyperactivity in childhood may diminish as a prominent symptom in adulthood, but the individual may still be impaired from ADHD.

Individuals with ADHD are at increased risk for negative driving outcomes. Also, texting significantly impairs the driving performance of all adolescents and increases driving related impairment in adolescents with ADHD.

Approximately 60% of adults with ADHD who take stimulant medication show moderate to marked improvement in their symptoms, including hyperactivity, inattention, mood lability, temper, disorganization, stress sensitivity, and impulsivity.
Significant growth changes are not seen in those with long-term use of stimulants or atomoxetine.
Stimulant therapy of ADHD has long-term beneficial effects and is well tolerated.

Parents and teachers should complete the Vanderbilt assessment follow-up within 3 months to 6 months of initiation of therapy for children. A short phone follow-up within the week of starting medication is important to determine treatment response and the presence of any adverse effects.
Reevaluate 4 to 8 weeks after the initiation of drug therapy. Inquire about sleep patterns and appetite, check weight, and look for the presence of tics. Evaluate at least quarterly thereafter.

After initiation of therapy in adults, schedule a monthly follow-up for behavioral response and adverse effects to medication. Increase the interval to every 3 months after a positive response is achieved.
Few studies have evaluated the long-term safety of drugs for ADHD. A systematic monitoring of long-term safety is needed.

Parents should: (1) avoid fatigue in children, (2) provide outlets for the release of the child's excess energy, (3) keep the home environment organized, (4) maintain consistent discipline and enforce with nonphysical punishment, (5) minimize formal gatherings, (6) accept child's limitations, and (7) continue to educate themselves about the condition.

Adolescents and adults should: (1) avoid alcohol, (2) be sure the duration of the medication covers the time while driving, (3) avoid fatigue, (4) exercise daily, and (5) continue to educate themselves on the condition.
The diagnosis of ADHD can be made with the criteria stated in .
Education and counseling should be the principal approach to treatment in pregnancy. Daily physical activity is advocated provided there is no contraindication because of pregnancy complications.
Because all drugs listed in are category C (risk cannot be ruled out), they should be avoided in pregnancy and also while breastfeeding.
There is no increased risk of ADHD with first trimester antidepressant use.
Prenatal supplementation with docosahexanoic (DHA) may contribute to improved sustained attention in preschool children.
Maternal use of triptans during pregnancy is not associated with risk of ADHD in children.

algorithm.title: General Approach to Children and Adolescents with Suspected ADHD.

cell.label: You suspect ADHD because of inattention, hyperactivity, impulsivity, academic underachievement, or behavior problems. Situational crisis?
Use Vanderbilt screening tool (http://www.nichq.org/adhd_tools.html) along with evaluating DSM-V criteria for ADHD.
Check home and school environment; consider counseling, referral, or other diagnoses.
Screen for other primary disorders and associated comorbidities (if present, consider neuropsychiatric testing).
Educate child, parent, and school; determine goals for therapy; regular physical activity; pharmacotherapy; focused counseling for child and parent may be needed; support groups (eg, CHADD).
Educate child, parent, and school; learning disorder may require accommodations; advocacy group (eg, CHADD); depending on complexity of comorbidities, may consult psychiatrist or psychologist.
Treat underlying condition. May require subspecialist referral.

algorithm.title: General Approach to Adults with Suspected ADHD.

cell.label: You suspect ADHD because of inattention, impulsivity and/or hyperactivity leading to pervasive impairment. Significant crisis?
Consider other etiology; ie, substance abuse, head trauma.
Is patient in school or going back to school, or in a profession where the possible use of a controlled substance needs to be documented?
Suggest neuropsychological testing and/or psychiatric consult if there's concern about any comorbidity.
Educate patient and family about disorder; daily exercise; pharmacotherapy; specialized counseling for comorbid issues or behavioral problems; participate in advocacy and support groups.

feature.caption: DSM-V Criteria for ADHD.
feature.feature_body:
Symptoms must occur often and have persisted for at least 6 months. At least 6 of 9 symptoms of inattention (ADHD, predominantly inattentive type), hyperactivity/ impulsivity (ADHD, predominantly hyperactive/impulsive type), or both (ADHD, combined type) are required for a classic diagnosis for full ADHD to be present. Inattention symptoms: Makes careless mistakes Has difficulty sustaining attention Appears not to listen Fails to complete tasks Disorganized Avoids tasks which require sustained attention Loses things Easily distracted Forgetful
Hyperactive-impulsive symptoms: Fiidgets with hands or feet or squirms in chair Has difficulty remaining seated Runs about or climbs excessively in children; extreme restlessness in adults Difficulty engaging in activities quietly Acts as if driven by a motor; adults will often feel like they were driven by a motor Talks excessively Blurts out answers before questions have been completed Difficulty waiting or taking turns Interrupts or intrudes upon others
Combined inattentive & hyperactive-impulsive symptoms: Has symptoms from both of the above symptom categories.
Some impairing symptoms were present before 12 years of age. Some impairment from symptoms in present in 2 or more settings (ie, school, home, or work). There must be clear evidence of clinically significant impairment in social, academic, or occupational functioning. Symptoms do not occur exclusively during course of a pervasive developmental disorder, schizophrenia, or other psychotic disorder and are not better accounted for by another mental disorder (ie, anxiety disorder, mood disorder, dissociative disorder, or personality disorder). From the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders DSM-V. Washington, DC: American Psychiatric Association, 2013.
